LESSONS.title: Applications and Digital Research: Quadratic Equations in the Real World

slo.purpose: Learners use digital devices or print resources to research real-world applications of quadratic equations — in architecture, agriculture, sports, and business — observing online safety measures. Small groups prepare short presentations linking their findings to the driving question. The teacher facilitates a gallery walk and class discussion. Learners add new connections to the DQB and revise their models of 'what a quadratic equation can tell us.'
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that quadratic equations model real-life situations in architecture (arch design, roof spans), agriculture (rectangular farm plots, irrigation channels), sports (trajectory of a ball), and business (profit-loss optimisation); and that the solutions of a quadratic equation correspond to meaningful (or non-meaningful) answers depending on context.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (i) use digital devices or print resources to research applications of quadratic equations while observing online safety measures; (ii) identify the quadratic relationship in a real-world situation and write the corresponding equation; (iii) prepare and deliver a short group presentation linking research findings to the driving question; (iv) critically evaluate which solution(s) of a quadratic equation are valid in a given real-life context.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate that quadratic equations are powerful tools for solving practical problems across many fields in Kenya and beyond, and will demonstrate respect, humility, and digital responsibility while collaborating and sharing findings with peers.
slo.keyInquiry: How are quadratic equations applied in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Achieng and her classmates have already formed and solved quadratic equations (Lessons 1–6). Now they ask: beyond the prize-giving chair arrangement, where else do people in Kenya use this mathematics? By researching architecture, agriculture, sports, and business, learners discover that the squared-unknown structure they puzzled over in Lesson 1 appears everywhere — from the curved roof of a Kisumu community hall to the optimal maize-planting layout on a Rift Valley farm. This lesson expands the driving question from 'how do we solve it?' to 'why does this equation keep appearing, and what does each solution tell us about the real world?'
slo.safetyNotes: Learners must observe online safety measures at all times: use only school-approved websites or the Kenya Education Cloud; do not share personal information online; report any inappropriate content to the teacher immediately. If physical devices are unavailable, pre-printed research cards are provided as an alternative.

LESSONS.overview: In this 80-minute lesson, learners work in small groups (4–5) to research real-world applications of quadratic equations across four domains — architecture, agriculture, sports, and business — using digital devices or print resource cards. Each group prepares a short poster-style presentation (or digital slide) linking their findings to the driving question. A structured gallery walk allows all groups to share evidence, after which the teacher facilitates a whole-class sensemaking discussion. Learners update the Driving Question Board (DQB) with new application connections and revise their cumulative models to reflect what quadratic equations reveal in each context. The lesson is anchored throughout to the Kisumu prize-giving phenomenon: just as Achieng's chair-arrangement problem produced x(x+7)=120, learners discover that the same structural pattern — a product of two related linear expressions equalling a known quantity — recurs across Kenyan real-life situations.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually write answers to two prompt questions in their exercise books (3 minutes silent writing): (1) 'Besides arranging chairs for Achieng's prize-giving ceremony, name ONE situation in Kenya where you think a quadratic equation might be useful — and explain why you think a squared term would appear.' (2) 'If solving a quadratic equation gives you two answers, say x = 8 and x = −15, what would you do with those two answers in a real-life problem?' Learners then share predictions with a partner (Think-Pair) for 2 minutes before selected pairs share with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Post the two prompt questions on the board before learners enter. Say: 'Before we research anything today, I want to know what YOU already think. Write your two answers silently — do not discuss yet. You have 3 minutes.' [Start timer. Maintain silence. After 3 minutes:] 'Now turn to your partner and share. You each have 1 minute.' [After pair share:] Cold-call FOUR pairs (aim for gender and ability mix) using the prompt: 'Wanjiku, what situation did you predict, and why does a squared term appear there?' Apply 10-second WAIT TIME before accepting any response. Record key predictions on the board under the heading 'Our Predictions — Before Research.' Do NOT confirm or correct yet — simply say: 'Interesting. Let's see what the evidence tells us.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with Prediction Recording — activates prior knowledge from Lessons 1–6, surfaces existing mental models, and creates a public 'prediction wall' against which post-research findings will be compared. This makes conceptual change visible and motivates the research phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each learner has written at least one plausible real-life context (architecture, farming, sports, business, etc.) and has articulated — however informally — why a product of two related quantities produces a squared term. Listen for learners who say only 'I don't know' — pair these with stronger predictors and note for targeted support during group research.

framework.phase: Phase 2 — Observe (Digital / Print Research + Group Poster Preparation)
framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in four home groups (assigned before the lesson), each researching one domain. Group A: Architecture (e.g., arch spans in Nairobi's KICC building, rectangular floor plans). Group B: Agriculture (e.g., optimal rectangular plot dimensions for a maize shamba in the Rift Valley, irrigation channel cross-sections). Group C: Sports (e.g., trajectory of a football kicked by Harambee Stars players at Kasarani Stadium — projectile motion producing h = −5t² + 20t + 1). Group D: Business (e.g., a Mombasa market trader's profit function P = −2x² + 80x − 300 where x is the number of units sold). Each group uses digital devices (Kenya Education Cloud / approved sites) OR a pre-printed research card (provided by teacher) to: (i) find or read one concrete example of their domain; (ii) identify the quadratic equation in that example; (iii) write down what the two solutions mean in context; (iv) create a poster or digital slide with: the real-life situation described in one sentence, the quadratic equation written clearly, the solutions found (by factorisation or other method from prior lessons), and a statement about which solution is valid and why. Groups have 20 minutes for research and 8 minutes for poster/slide preparation.
framework.teacherMoves:
Distribute research cards and confirm device access (2 min). Say: 'Each group has a different real-world domain. Your job is to find a genuine example, write the quadratic equation it produces, solve it, and decide which answer makes sense in real life — just like Achieng had to choose between her two answers for the chairs. You have 20 minutes to research, then 8 minutes to prepare your poster. Online safety rule: only approved sites or the Kenya Education Cloud. If you see anything inappropriate, tell me immediately.' [Circulate every 4–5 minutes. At each group, ask ONE probing question — see below — then move on.] Probing questions by group: Group A (Architecture): 'If the width of the arch is w metres and the length exceeds the width by 5 m, and the area is 84 m², what equation does that give you?' Group B (Agriculture): 'Farmer Wambua has a rectangular shamba. The length is 3 m more than the width and the area is 180 m². Write the equation for the width.' Group C (Sports): 'At what time does the ball hit the ground? What do you do with the negative time answer?' Group D (Business): 'At what number of units sold is the profit zero? Which of the two values makes business sense?' At 25 minutes: give a 3-minute warning: 'Three minutes left for research — move to poster preparation.' Remind groups: 'Your poster must show the equation clearly — a person walking past must be able to read and understand it without you explaining.'

At 5 minutes remaining in poster prep: 'One minute — finalise your title and the sentence about which solution is valid.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Jigsaw Research with Domain Specialisation — each group becomes the class 'expert' on one application domain. This distributes the cognitive load of exploring multiple contexts while ensuring all learners receive full breadth of applications through the gallery walk that follows. Anchoring each domain to a Kenyan context (Kasarani, Rift Valley shamba, Mombasa market) keeps the research relevant and the phenomenon central.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators during circulation: (1) The group's written equation is correctly formed (quadratic, not linear). (2) At least one group member can explain verbally why the squared term arises (product of two related unknowns). (3) The group has identified which solution is not valid in context (e.g., negative length, negative time) — this is the key conceptual target for this lesson. Flag any group whose equation is linear or whose poster does not address solution validity for whole-class discussion in Phase 3.

framework.phase: Phase 3 — Explain (Gallery Walk + Whole-Class Sensemaking Discussion)
framework.learnerExperience: Posters are displayed around the room (or slides projected in rotation). Learners conduct a structured gallery walk (10 minutes): each group visits the other three posters, leaving one 'star' sticky note (something correct and clear) and one 'arrow' sticky note (a question or suggestion). After the gallery walk, learners return to their seats. The teacher leads a 15-minute whole-class discussion synthesising findings across all four domains. Learners record in their exercise books: 'The quadratic structure that appeared in Achieng's chair problem (rows × columns = 120, where columns = rows + 7) also appears in [architecture / agriculture / sports / business] because ____.' Learners then answer the critical question: 'In Achieng's problem, one solution was x = 8 (rows) and the other was x = −15. Why did we reject x = −15? Give a parallel example from today's research where one solution is rejected — and state why.'
framework.teacherMoves: Gallery Walk Setup (1 min): 'Each group will visit the other three posters. Leave a STAR sticky note — one thing that is mathematically correct and clearly explained. Leave an ARROW sticky note — one question you have OR one thing that could be improved. You have 10 minutes. Move quietly and read carefully.' [Time the gallery walk strictly. At 9 minutes: '1 minute remaining — return to your posters and read the notes left for you.'] Whole-class discussion (15 min): Stand at the board with the prediction list from Phase 1. Say: 'Let us now compare what we predicted with what the research showed.' Point to each prediction and ask: 'Did the evidence support this, extend it, or challenge it?' Cold-call SIX learners across the four groups. After each response, apply 12-second WAIT TIME before commenting. Key questions to pose in sequence: (Q1) 'What is the ONE thing all four examples have in common mathematically?' [Target: a product of two related linear expressions equals a known constant, producing x² + bx + c = 0.] (Q2) 'Group C, your sports example gave a negative time as one solution. Group A, your architecture example gave a negative length. Why does mathematics produce these answers if they are not physically possible?' [Target: the equation describes a broader mathematical relationship; context filters valid solutions.] (Q3) 'Connect back to Kisumu: Achieng rejected x = −15 rows. Based on today's research, write a general rule for when we reject a quadratic solution in a real-life problem.' Write learner-generated rule on the board verbatim, then refine collaboratively. Say: 'This rule — rejecting solutions that contradict physical or contextual constraints — is one of the most important mathematical habits of mind you will use throughout your lives.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery Walk with Star-Arrow Protocol followed by Socratic Whole-Class Discussion — the gallery walk externalises peer assessment and surfaces misconceptions before whole-class discussion. The Socratic sequence (Q1→Q2→Q3) moves learners from noticing surface similarities across examples, to understanding why extraneous solutions arise, to constructing a general rule. This mirrors the NGSS practice of constructing explanations from evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) During gallery walk, arrow sticky notes reveal genuine mathematical questions (not just spelling corrections) — collect these for Q&A. (2) During Q1 discussion, learners use the phrase 'product of two related expressions' or equivalent — if absent, re-prompt. (3) For Q3, learners can state: 'We reject a solution if it gives a negative length, area, time, or quantity, because these have no physical meaning in the problem.' Learners who cannot connect to the phenomenon (Achieng's x = −15) need targeted support — note their names for follow-up in Phase 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners spend 8 minutes updating the class DQB. Each group adds: (i) one new APPLICATION card (domain + Kenyan context + equation structure, e.g., 'Agriculture — Rift Valley maize shamba: w(w+3) = 180'); (ii) one ANSWER card that responds to a previously posted question on the DQB (from Lessons 1–6) if their research provides evidence for it; and (iii) one NEW QUESTION card that their research raised (e.g., 'Can quadratic equations model situations where the answer is never a whole number?'). Individually, each learner also writes in their exercise book: 'Before Lesson 7, I thought quadratic equations were only useful for ____. Now I know they also apply to ____ because ____.'
framework.teacherMoves: Direct learners to the DQB: 'You have 8 minutes. Each group adds three cards — an APPLICATION card, an ANSWER card for something we wondered before, and a NEW QUESTION card your research raised. Write clearly so the whole class can read from a distance.' [Circulate and read cards as they go up. If an application card lacks an equation, prompt: 'Can you add the equation structure next to your context?'] After 8 minutes, read aloud THREE new application cards and ONE new question card, chosen to represent different domains. Say: 'Notice how the DQB is growing — when Achieng first drew her chair layout in Lesson 1, we had one question. Now we have evidence from architecture, agriculture, sports, and business. Our model of what a quadratic equation can do is getting much bigger.' Point to the Before/After reflection in learners' books: 'This reflection is evidence of YOUR thinking changing. That is what learning looks like.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Public Knowledge-Building on the DQB — making individual and group thinking visible on the DQB creates a shared class knowledge artefact that tracks conceptual growth across the entire 8-lesson sequence. The Before/After reflection prompts metacognition, helping learners recognise their own conceptual change, a key CBE competency (learning to learn).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) APPLICATION cards contain a correctly structured equation (not just a description). (2) ANSWER cards cite specific evidence from today's research ('Group B found that…'). (3) NEW QUESTION cards are mathematically grounded, not vague. (4) Before/After reflections show a genuine expansion of scope (from one context to multiple contexts). Collect exercise books of three learners (one from each performance band) to read Before/After reflections as informal diagnostic data before Lesson 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually revise their cumulative model (started in Lesson 1 and updated in each subsequent lesson). Today's revision must add: (a) at least TWO new real-life domains where quadratic equations appear, with a labelled arrow showing how the domain connects to the general form ax² + bx + c = 0; (b) a 'solution validity filter' box — a visual reminder that real-life constraints (no negative lengths, areas, times, or quantities) determine which mathematical solution is physically meaningful; and (c) a revised answer (or a more nuanced answer) to the driving question written at the top of the model page: 'How can writing and solving a quadratic equation help us find unknown dimensions, quantities, and arrangements in real-life situations across Kenya?' Learners have 10 minutes. At the end, two volunteers share their revised models under the visualiser or by holding them up, and the class gives one piece of 'warm' and one piece of 'cool' feedback per model.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your cumulative models. In Lessons 1 to 6 you built a model of what a quadratic equation is and how to solve it. Today you discovered WHERE it lives in the real world. Add at least two domains with arrows to the general form, add a solution-validity filter box, and write a better answer to our driving question at the top. You have 10 minutes — work in silence.' [Circulate for first 5 minutes, noting learners who are not adding new domains — prompt: 'Which of the four groups' examples could YOU add to your model? Choose one and draw the arrow.'] At 10 minutes: 'Two volunteers — who will share?' Cold-call if no volunteers. For each model shared, facilitate class feedback: 'One warm — something strong about this model. One cool — one suggestion.' Record the driving-question answers written by both volunteers on the board. Say: 'Compare these two answers to what Achieng's classmates said in Lesson 1. Has your class's understanding of the driving question grown? I think it has. In Lesson 8, we will bring everything together for our final response.' End with: 'Achieng's chair problem was one arrangement in Kisumu. Today you showed it is also a roof in Nairobi, a shamba in the Rift Valley, a goal kick at Kasarani, and a market stall in Mombasa. That is the power of algebra.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Peer Feedback — iterative model revision is an NGSS Science and Engineering Practice (Developing and Using Models) adapted for mathematics. Each revision cycle makes the model more complete and more connected. The solution-validity filter box targets the key conceptual hurdle of this lesson: that mathematics produces solutions the real world must judge. Peer warm/cool feedback develops communication and collaboration competencies mandated by KICD.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Model contains labelled arrows from at least two new real-life domains to the general quadratic form. (2) Solution-validity filter box is present and contains at least one example (e.g., 'negative length → reject'). (3) Revised driving-question answer explicitly mentions multiple domains and the idea of choosing between solutions based on context. (4) Learners who produced models with no new domains or no filter box are flagged for targeted review at the start of Lesson 8.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) Did all four groups produce a correctly formed quadratic equation from their research domain — or did any group produce a linear equation instead? If so, what misconception drove that, and how will you address it in Lesson 8's consolidation? (2) During the gallery walk, what did the arrow sticky notes reveal about gaps in learners' understanding of solution validity? Were learners able to articulate WHY a negative solution is rejected, or did they simply say 'it doesn't make sense'? (3) How effectively did learners connect their research findings back to the Kisumu chair-arrangement phenomenon? If the connection was weak, consider opening Lesson 8 with an explicit comparison table: Achieng's problem vs. each of the four research domains, column by column. (4) Review the Before/After reflections from the three exercise books collected. Do learners demonstrate genuine conceptual expansion, or are they restating the same single context? Use this to calibrate the depth of consolidation needed in Lesson 8. (5) Was the 80-minute timing sufficient? If the gallery walk ran over, consider reducing Phase 1 (Predict) to 4 minutes in future by posting prompt questions as a warm-up task before class begins.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners researched and identified real-world examples of quadratic equations in architecture (e.g., rectangular floor plans and arch spans in Nairobi), agriculture (e.g., rectangular maize shamba dimensions in the Rift Valley), sports (e.g., football trajectory at Kasarani Stadium), and business (e.g., a Mombasa market trader's profit function). They observed that in each case, a product of two related linear expressions — equal to a known total — generates a quadratic equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners learned that: (i) the quadratic structure first seen in Achieng's chair problem (rows × columns = 120, where columns exceed rows by 7) recurs across many real-life domains in Kenya; (ii) solving a quadratic equation produces two mathematical solutions, but real-life context (no negative lengths, areas, times, or quantities) determines which solution is physically valid; (iii) observing online safety measures is a responsibility when using digital devices for mathematical research; and (iv) quadratic equations are a tool for decision-making — in design, farming, sport, and commerce.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained why a squared unknown appears in real-life problems: whenever two related unknown quantities are multiplied together to give a known area, total, or quantity, the relationship produces a quadratic equation. They also explained the solution-validity rule: after solving by factorisation, substitute both solutions back into the real-life context and reject any solution that contradicts physical constraints (e.g., you cannot have a negative number of rows of chairs, a negative field width, or a negative time). This rule was connected explicitly to Achieng's rejection of x = −15 in Lesson 1's phenomenon.

LESSONS.title: Model Building, Consolidation & Final Explanation: The Full Journey of a Quadratic Equation

slo.purpose: Learners consolidate the entire sub-strand by constructing a cumulative visual model (poster or digital slide) that maps the full journey from real-life context → algebraic expression → quadratic expression → quadratic equation → factorisation → solution → interpretation in context. They present models, close the Driving Question Board, complete a written assessment, and articulate how quadratic equations are used across careers in Kenya.
slo.knowledge: Learners demonstrate understanding that: (a) real-life situations involving two related unknown dimensions whose product is known can be modelled by quadratic equations; (b) a quadratic equation of the form x² + bx + c = 0 is solved by factorisation; (c) both solutions must be tested against the real-life context, and solutions that are negative or otherwise impossible must be rejected; (d) quadratic equations appear across Kenyan careers including architecture, agriculture, event management, and engineering.
slo.skills: Learners are able to: (a) form algebraic expressions and quadratic equations from real-life scenarios; (b) factorise quadratic expressions and solve quadratic equations by the factor method; (c) interpret both solutions of a quadratic equation in context; (d) construct and present a cumulative visual model showing every stage of the problem-solving journey; (e) evaluate peers' models using a structured rubric.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that mathematics is not an isolated school subject but a tool embedded in everyday Kenyan life — from arranging chairs at Kisumu prize-giving ceremonies to designing rectangular shamba plots in Kericho and planning market stalls in Gikomba. Learners display respect by listening to peers' presentations without interruption, and demonstrate responsibility by submitting an honest individual written assessment.
slo.keyInquiry: How are quadratic equations applied in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson of the sub-strand. Achieng's seating-arrangement problem — which launched the unit — is fully resolved. Learners have now travelled the complete journey: they noticed a pattern that could not be solved by simple division, named it as a quadratic relationship, formed and factorised the equation, found two solutions, and interpreted which one makes sense for 120 chairs. In this lesson they make that entire journey visible in a single model, present it to the class, close every question on the Driving Question Board, and demonstrate mastery through a written class activity / assessment task.
slo.safetyNotes: If learners use scissors or cutting tools when constructing paper poster models, they must handle sharp edges carefully and work on a stable surface. Learners using shared digital devices must observe online safety guidelines (KICD PCIs) — they must not navigate to unrelated or unsafe websites while searching for career applications of quadratic equations.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 8 is the culminating lesson of Sub-Strand 1.3. It opens by returning directly to the phenomenon: Mr Otieno's challenge to Achieng — arrange 120 chairs in a rectangle where columns exceed rows by 7. In the Predict phase, learners revisit their Lesson 1 predictions and compare them with what they now know. In the Observe phase, small groups examine all their completed work from Lessons 1–7 and identify the complete solution pathway displayed on a class Evidence Wall. In the Explain phase, learners construct a cumulative journey poster/digital slide in groups, then present their Final Explanation of the driving question. The DQB review follows, where every sticky note is addressed. The lesson closes with an individual written class activity / assessment task drawn from the KICD-suggested assessment rubric, covering all four ability indicators for Sub-Strand 1.3. The teacher facilitates a closing career-connection discussion linking quadratic equations to real Kenyan professions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners receive back their original Lesson 1 prediction cards (or notebooks) showing their very first attempt to solve Achieng's problem — arranging 120 chairs in a rectangle where columns exceed rows by 7. Individually (3 minutes), they read their original prediction silently. They then write two sentences on a sticky note: (1) what they predicted then, and (2) what they now know. Pairs share their sticky notes for 2 minutes before whole-class sharing.
framework.teacherMoves:
BEFORE CLASS: Retrieve all Lesson 1 prediction cards / notebook entries and place one on each desk face-down. Display the phenomenon slide: 'Achieng at Kisumu school needs to arrange 120 chairs — columns exceed rows by 7. What are the dimensions?' 

Say verbatim: 'Turn over your card. Read what you wrote in Lesson 1. Do NOT change it — that is your evidence of how your thinking has grown.' 

WAIT TIME: Allow 3 full minutes of silent individual reading and writing. 

After pairs share, cold-call 3 learners (choose one who originally guessed and checked, one who left it blank, one who attempted algebra). Ask each: 'What do you know NOW that you did not know THEN?' 

Record three key before/after contrasts on the board in a T-chart labelled 'Lesson 1 thinking | Lesson 8 thinking'. Leave this visible for the full lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Before/After Prediction Comparison — Learners make their own cognitive growth visible by holding their original prediction alongside their current understanding. This activates metacognition and motivates the upcoming consolidation: they can SEE what the unit taught them.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Can each learner articulate at least one specific thing they now understand that they did not in Lesson 1? Listen for phrases such as 'I now know why there is an x-squared term' or 'I know to reject the negative solution because you cannot have negative rows.' If a learner cannot articulate any growth, note them for targeted support during Phase 3.

framework.phase: Phase 2 — Observe: Evidence Wall Gallery Walk
framework.learnerExperience: Around the classroom walls, the teacher has pre-posted six labelled Evidence Stations from the unit, each with key artefacts or summary cards: Station 1 — Real-life context (Achieng's chairs, shamba dimensions, market stalls); Station 2 — Forming algebraic expressions (representing rows as x, columns as x + 7); Station 3 — Forming quadratic equations (x(x+7)=120 → x²+7x−120=0); Station 4 — Factorisation method (finding factor pairs of −120 that sum to +7: +15 and −8); Station 5 — Solutions (x = 8 or x = −15) and interpretation (reject x = −15; rows = 8, columns = 15); Station 6 — Careers in Kenya that use quadratic equations. Groups of 4 (pre-assigned) rotate through all 6 stations in 12 minutes (2 minutes each), adding one sticky note per station: something they CONFIRM they understand and one question they still have.
framework.teacherMoves:
Before the gallery walk, say verbatim: 'You are not tourists — you are quality checkers. At each station, your group must agree on one thing you are CERTAIN about and one thing that still puzzles you. Write both on sticky notes and post them at the station.' 

Set a timer visible to all. Call 'Rotate!' every 2 minutes with a clap signal. 

Circulate continuously. At Station 3 (forming the equation), pause with each group and ask: 'Why is the equation NOT just 7x = 120? What changes when the unknown appears in BOTH dimensions?' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. Cold-call 2 groups to respond aloud. 

At Station 5 (interpretation), ask: 'Achieng found x = 8 and x = −15. She only used one. Which one and why?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners by name. 

After the walk, spend 3 minutes harvesting 'still puzzled' sticky notes. Read 3 aloud and tell the class: 'We will answer all of these before this lesson ends.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence Wall Gallery Walk — By moving through physical stations that sequence the unit's content chronologically, learners reconstruct the logic of the full journey. The sticky-note protocol makes thinking public and identifies gaps before the model-building phase. This mirrors the NGSS Science and Engineering Practice of 'Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information.'
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) Sticky notes at Station 3 correctly name the quadratic structure (look for 'x times x gives x-squared'); (b) Sticky notes at Station 5 correctly identify x = 8 as the valid solution with a real-life reason; (c) Groups that still confuse 'factorising' with 'expanding' are noted — teacher provides a targeted prompt card at their table before Phase 3 begins.

framework.phase: Phase 3 — Explain: Cumulative Journey Model Construction & Presentation (Final Explanation)
framework.learnerExperience: Each group (same groups of 4 from Phase 2) constructs a Cumulative Journey Model — a poster (A2 paper with markers) or a 6-slide digital presentation on a shared device. The model must include ALL seven labelled stages with arrows showing the direction of reasoning: (1) Real-life Context → (2) Identifying the Unknowns → (3) Forming the Algebraic Expression → (4) Forming the Quadratic Equation → (5) Factorising the Expression → (6) Solving for x → (7) Interpreting the Solution in Context. Each stage must include: the mathematical notation, a sentence in plain English, and a Kenya-relevant example from the unit (Achieng's chairs, OR a shamba plot, OR a market-stall scenario). Groups have 15 minutes to build. Each group then presents their model to the class in 3 minutes. Peer groups use a simple 3-point rubric card (provided by the teacher) to score: correctness of mathematics, clarity of the journey, and strength of real-life interpretation.
framework.teacherMoves:
Distribute large A2 paper or ensure each group's device is open to a blank slide deck. Say verbatim: 'Your model must tell the FULL story — from the moment Achieng could not solve her problem by guessing, all the way to the moment she told the head teacher: 8 rows, 15 columns. Every arrow matters. Every stage needs BOTH the algebra AND the plain-English sentence.' 

During construction (15 minutes), circulate with two priority questions: 
(a) 'Show me where in your model the squared term FIRST appears — why does it appear there?' 
(b) 'Where does your model show that one solution was rejected — and why?' 
WAIT TIME: 12 seconds after each prompt before accepting responses. 

During presentations, stand at the back so learners present TO the class, not to the teacher. After each presentation, ask the audience: 'What is ONE thing this group explained better than your own group?' Cold-call 2 audience members per presentation. 

After all presentations, facilitate a 5-minute whole-class convergence discussion. Ask: 'Looking at all models — what is the ONE stage that EVERY group agrees is the most important and WHY?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds. Record the consensus answer on the board. (Expected answer: Stage 4 — forming the quadratic equation — because without it, the rest of the journey cannot begin.)
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Journey Modelling with Peer Presentation — This is the primary sensemaking strategy for a final lesson. By constructing an artefact that makes the full reasoning chain visible, learners synthesise seven lessons of learning into a single coherent narrative. Peer scoring activates critical evaluation (NGSS Practice: Constructing Explanations). The convergence discussion builds shared disciplinary understanding of what a 'complete solution' means in mathematics.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators during model construction: (a) Stage 4 (forming the equation) uses correct notation x²+7x−120=0 and not x+7=120; (b) Stage 5 (factorisation) shows the correct factor pair (+15, −8) with working; (c) Stage 7 explicitly states that x = −15 is rejected because a negative number of rows has no real-life meaning. During presentations: listen for learners who can explain WHY, not just WHAT — 'The squared term appears because we multiply rows by columns, and the unknown appears in BOTH dimensions.'

framework.phase: Phase 4 — DQB Review: Closing Every Question on the Driving Question Board
framework.learnerExperience: The class Driving Question Board (DQB) — which has been built up across all 8 lessons — is displayed at the front. The teacher reads each sticky-note question aloud, one by one. For each question, the class votes silently: thumbs up = 'we can fully answer this now'; thumbs sideways = 'we can partially answer this'; thumbs down = 'we still cannot answer this.' For every 'thumbs up' question, a volunteer learner provides the answer in one or two sentences, which the teacher writes on a green card and sticks over the original question. For 'thumbs sideways' and 'thumbs down' questions, the teacher acknowledges them honestly and, where appropriate, notes which future topic (e.g., quadratic formula in Grade 11) will address them. The class also revisits the three overarching questions that launched the unit: 'Why does a seating problem produce a squared term?', 'How do you solve an equation where the unknown is multiplied by itself?', and 'When you find two answers, which one works — or do both?'
framework.teacherMoves:
Stand beside the DQB. Say verbatim: 'Every question on this board was asked by someone in this class. Every question was a good question. Let us honour each one with a proper answer.' 

Read each question slowly. After the class votes, for 'thumbs up' questions say: 'Who will answer this for us in one sentence?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. Cold-call the learner who originally posted that question wherever possible — give them the honour of answering their own question. 

For the three anchor questions of the unit, call on 3 different learners per question. Prompt: 'Use the words ROWS, COLUMNS, PRODUCT, and SQUARED TERM in your answer.' 

For unresolved questions, model intellectual honesty: 'This is a real question that mathematics has an answer to — we will meet it again when we study the quadratic formula in Grade 11.' Write those questions on a 'Further Inquiry' strip and post it on the wall. 

Close the DQB review by asking the whole class: 'How has our driving question — how can writing and solving a quadratic equation help us find unknown dimensions, quantities, and arrangements in real-life Kenya? — been answered today?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB Closure with Collective Verification — The DQB has tracked growing understanding across the unit. Closing it publicly creates a shared record of what the class now knows and what remains open. This mirrors scientific practice: claims are revisited, tested against evidence, and either confirmed or identified as requiring further investigation. The 'Further Inquiry' strip models the disposition of a lifelong learner.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) At least 80% of DQB questions receive 'thumbs up' votes, suggesting whole-class understanding; (b) Learners can answer the three anchor questions using correct mathematical vocabulary (product, squared term, factorisation, rejection of negative solution); (c) Any learner still uncertain about the distinction between 'forming the expression' and 'forming the equation' is noted for individual follow-up after the assessment task.

framework.phase: Phase 5 — Model Building / Written Assessment: Individual Class Activity & Career Connections
framework.learnerExperience: PART A — Individual Written Assessment (20 minutes): Each learner completes a structured class activity / assessment task independently and in silence. The task contains four sections aligned to the KICD assessment rubric indicators: (i) Form a quadratic expression: 'A rectangular maize shamba in Kericho has an area of 180 m². The length exceeds the width by 3 m. Write an expression for the area in terms of the width w.' (ii) Form a quadratic equation: 'Using your expression, write a quadratic equation and rearrange it into the standard form w² + bw + c = 0.' (iii) Factorise and solve: 'Factorise the quadratic expression and solve the equation.' (iv) Interpret and apply: 'State which solution is valid for the shamba and give its dimensions. Explain why the other solution cannot apply.' PART B — Career Connections Discussion (10 minutes): After submitting the assessment, learners participate in a structured Think-Pair-Share. Prompt: 'Name one Kenyan career where a professional would NEED to solve a quadratic equation, and describe a specific situation in that career where the equation would arise.' Pairs share for 2 minutes, then 6 pairs report to the whole class. Teacher records career examples on the board.
framework.teacherMoves:
Distribute printed or handwritten assessment task sheets. Say verbatim: 'This is your chance to show EVERYTHING you have learned across all eight lessons. Show every step — forming the expression, writing the equation, factorising, solving, and interpreting. A correct final answer with no working earns you very few marks. The JOURNEY is what is being assessed.' 

During the 20-minute assessment, circulate silently. Do NOT answer mathematical questions — instead, if a learner is stuck, point silently to the relevant stage of their journey model poster (still visible on the wall). 

After assessment papers are collected, transition to Part B. Say: 'Quadratic equations are not only in Achieng's school in Kisumu. They show up wherever two related quantities multiply to give a fixed total. Think about a farmer in Kericho, an architect designing a block of flats in Nairobi, a market organiser setting up stalls in Gikomba, or a fish farmer at Lake Victoria.' 

For Think-Pair-Share: WAIT TIME 2 minutes for individual thinking before pairs discuss. Cold-call 6 pairs — aim for gender balance and varied career sectors. Record each career on the board. 

Close the lesson with a whole-class statement. Say verbatim: 'Every career on this board is a career that is open to you. The mathematics you have learned in this sub-strand is not a school exercise — it is a professional tool. Achieng solved her seating problem. What problem will YOU solve with it?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Written Assessment as Final Model Revision — The assessment task is itself the final act of model building: learners apply the complete problem-solving journey independently to a NEW but structurally identical context (Kericho shamba). This confirms whether the understanding is transferable, not just recallable. The career-connections discussion connects disciplinary knowledge to identity and aspiration — a key dimension of KICD's CBE competency of 'self-efficacy' and the National Goal of promoting individual development and self-fulfilment.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators for summative use: (a) Section (i): correct quadratic expression w(w+3) or w²+3w — no marks if learner writes w+3=180; (b) Section (ii): equation correctly rearranged to w²+3w−180=0; (c) Section (iii): correct factorisation (w+15)(w−12)=0 yielding w=12 or w=−15; (d) Section (iv): valid solution stated as w=12 m (width), length=15 m, with explicit rejection of w=−15 on grounds that width cannot be negative. KICD rubric level: Exceeds Expectations = all four sections correct with explanation; Meets Expectations = all four sections correct; Approaches Expectations = any two of four correct; Below Expectations = any one of four correct.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After delivering this lesson, reflect on the following four questions and record your notes in your professional journal:

1. JOURNEY VISIBILITY: When learners presented their cumulative journey models, were all seven stages present and correctly connected with arrows? Which stage was most commonly missing or incorrect? (Common gap: Stage 7 — learners solve correctly but fail to explicitly reject the negative solution in writing.) How will you address this in Lesson 1 of the next sub-strand by building the habit of always interpreting solutions in context?

2. DQB CLOSURE: Were there questions on the DQB that the class could not answer by 'thumbs up'? List them. Do these questions suggest a gap in your teaching sequence, or do they represent genuine Grade 11 content (e.g., quadratic formula, completing the square)? If a majority of the class gave 'thumbs down' to a question that should have been answered in this unit, plan a 10-minute retrieval activity at the start of the next lesson.

3. ASSESSMENT QUALITY: In the individual written assessment (the Kericho shamba task), how many learners reached Section (iv) — interpretation — and rejected the negative solution with a written reason? The KICD rubric indicator for 'Exceeds Expectations' requires learners to explain each step with varied examples. If fewer than 60% of learners reached this level, consider whether your Phase 3 model-building activity provided enough practice with interpretation before the formal assessment.

4. CAREER CONNECTIONS: Which careers did learners name in Part B? Were the responses specific (e.g., 'A fisheries officer at Lake Victoria calculates the dimensions of a rectangular fish pond to maximise area for a given fencing perimeter') or generic (e.g., 'engineers use maths')? If responses were generic, plan a 5-minute career-context starter activity at the beginning of your next sub-strand to deepen learners' awareness of mathematics in Kenyan professional life.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Students examined an Evidence Wall of six stations tracing the complete unit journey — from Achieng's 120-chair seating problem at a Kisumu school to the factorised solution and real-life interpretation. They identified which solution (x = 8 rows) is valid and why x = −15 must be rejected.

It is solved by finding factor pairs of the constant term whose sum equals the coefficient of x. Both solutions must be tested in context — negative values are rejected because physical quantities such as rows and columns cannot be negative.

They presented these models, closed the Driving Question Board, completed an individual written assessment task (Kericho shamba dimensions), and connected quadratic equations to careers across Kenya including architecture, agriculture, event management, and fisheries.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Essential Mathematics – Grade 10 | Sub-strand 1.3: Quadratic Equations
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: This is your Final Explanation document. Use it as a model to help you write a complete, well-organised answer to the driving question. Read each section carefully, study the exemplar responses, and use them as a guide when you write your own answer. Your goal is to show that you truly understand how quadratic equations connect to real-life situations — not just how to solve them on paper. Write in full sentences, use correct mathematical vocabulary, and always check whether your answer makes sense in context.

sections.title: Section 1: Identify the Real-Life Situation and Define the Unknown
sections.prompt: Describe the real-life problem in your own words. What quantity is unknown? How do you assign a variable to represent it? Why can't you solve this problem with simple division or a one-step calculation?
sections.exemplar: Achieng's school in Kisumu needs to seat 120 guests in a rectangular arrangement of chairs. The number of columns exceeds the number of rows by 7, but neither the number of rows nor columns is known. Because the two unknowns are related — one is 7 more than the other — and because their product must equal 120, you cannot find the answer by simply dividing 120 by a single number. You need to represent one unknown with a variable. Let the number of rows = x. Then the number of columns = x + 7. This step is critical: choosing a clear variable definition keeps your equation meaningful and prevents confusion later. Whenever a problem involves two related quantities whose product (or sum of products) gives a fixed total, a single variable and a quadratic equation are the right tools to use.

sections.title: Section 2: Write and Justify the Quadratic Equation
sections.prompt: Write the equation that models the situation. Show every step of forming the equation. Explain why the equation contains a squared term — in other words, where does the 'quadratic' part come from in this real-life context?
sections.exemplar: Since rows × columns = total chairs, you can write: x(x + 7) = 120. Expanding the left side gives x² + 7x = 120, which rearranges to x² + 7x − 120 = 0. The squared term (x²) appears because you are multiplying two expressions that both contain the variable x — rows and columns are each described using x, so their product naturally produces x². This is what makes the equation quadratic rather than linear. A linear equation would appear if only one dimension contained the unknown, but here both dimensions depend on x, so the equation must have degree 2. Recognising this structure is the key insight: any time two related lengths, quantities, or dimensions are multiplied together to give a fixed area or total, a quadratic equation is the correct model.

sections.title: Section 3: Solve the Quadratic Equation and Interpret Both Roots
sections.prompt: Solve your equation using an appropriate method (factorisation, completing the square, or the quadratic formula). Show all working clearly. You will get two solutions — explain what each solution means in the real-life context and decide which solution is valid.
sections.exemplar: Starting from x² + 7x − 120 = 0, you look for two numbers that multiply to −120 and add to +7. Those numbers are +15 and −8, so the equation factorises as (x + 15)(x − 8) = 0. Setting each factor equal to zero gives x = −15 or x = 8. Now you must interpret both roots in context. x = −15 means there would be −15 rows of chairs. A negative number of rows is physically impossible — you cannot have a negative count of chairs in a hall in Kisumu or anywhere else. Therefore x = −15 is rejected. x = 8 is positive and realistic: 8 rows of chairs, and 8 + 7 = 15 columns of chairs. Checking: 8 × 15 = 120 ✓. The valid solution is 8 rows and 15 columns. This step — checking both roots against the real-life constraints — is just as important as the algebra itself. In many practical problems, one root will be mathematically correct but contextually meaningless.

sections.title: Section 4: Connect the Mathematics to the Broader Driving Question
sections.prompt: Go beyond Achieng's seating problem. Explain how the same process — defining a variable, writing a quadratic equation, solving it, and interpreting the roots — applies to at least ONE other real-life situation in Kenya. Use a specific, detailed example.
sections.exemplar: The same quadratic thinking applies to many everyday situations across Kenya. Consider a maize farmer in the Rift Valley who wants to enclose a rectangular shamba using 54 metres of fencing, and needs the enclosed area to be exactly 180 m². If the width of the shamba is w metres, then the length is (27 − w) metres (since 2w + 2l = 54, so l = 27 − w). The area condition gives w(27 − w) = 180, which expands to 27w − w² = 180, or w² − 27w + 180 = 0. Factorising: (w − 12)(w − 15) = 0, giving w = 12 or w = 15. Both roots are positive and realistic here — a 12 m × 15 m shamba or a 15 m × 12 m shamba are the same rectangle described from different sides. Both roots are valid, which shows that context determines whether one or both solutions are accepted. In each case, the process is identical: name the unknown, form the product, expand, rearrange to standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, solve, and interpret. Quadratic equations are therefore a powerful and flexible tool for any Kenyan context involving areas, arrangements, or two related quantities multiplied together.

sections.title: Section 5: Reflect on Your Learning and the Power of Quadratic Equations
sections.prompt: Look back at the full sequence of lessons. What was confusing at the start that now makes sense? What is the most important idea you are taking away about quadratic equations? How has your thinking changed from Lesson 1 to now?
sections.exemplar: At the start of this sequence, Achieng's problem seemed confusing — it was hard to see why a seating arrangement would produce an equation with x². Now it is clear: whenever two unknown but related quantities are multiplied together, the result is always a quadratic expression. The most important idea to take away is that quadratic equations are not just abstract algebra — they are a language for describing real situations involving area, dimensions, and arrangements. A second key insight is that getting two solutions is not a mistake; it is a feature of quadratic equations, and your job is always to test both solutions against the real-life context to decide which one (or sometimes both) make sense. Finally, the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 is a tool: rearranging every quadratic into this form before solving makes it easier to choose the right method — factorisation when the numbers work out neatly, completing the square when they do not, or the quadratic formula when you need a guaranteed method. These skills transfer directly to future topics such as quadratic graphs, projectile motion in Physics, and financial calculations in Business Studies.

rubric.criterion: Defining the Unknown and Setting Up the Variable
rubric.excellent: Clearly and correctly defines the variable with explicit units or context (e.g., 'Let x = the number of rows of chairs'). Explains in precise language why a single variable is sufficient to describe both unknowns and why simple division cannot solve the problem.
rubric.proficient: Correctly defines the variable and links it to the second unknown (x + 7). Mentions why the problem cannot be solved by division alone, though the explanation may lack full depth.
rubric.developing: Attempts to define a variable but the definition is vague, incorrect, or disconnected from the context. May attempt to solve by trial and error without forming an equation.

rubric.criterion: Forming and Justifying the Quadratic Equation
rubric.excellent: Accurately writes x(x + 7) = 120, expands fully, and rearranges to standard form x² + 7x − 120 = 0 with all steps shown. Clearly explains that the squared term arises from multiplying two expressions both containing x, and uses the term 'quadratic' correctly.
rubric.proficient: Correctly forms and expands the equation to standard form with minor arithmetic slips that do not affect understanding. Gives a reasonable explanation of why the equation is quadratic.
rubric.developing: Sets up the equation with errors (e.g., writes x + (x + 7) = 120 instead of a product) or fails to rearrange to standard form. Explanation of the squared term is absent or incorrect.

rubric.criterion: Solving the Equation and Interpreting Both Roots
rubric.excellent: Solves the equation correctly using a valid method (factorisation, completing the square, or quadratic formula) with all working shown. Explicitly interprets both roots in context, clearly explains why x = −15 is rejected, verifies x = 8 by substitution (8 × 15 = 120), and states the final answer in a full sentence.
rubric.proficient: Obtains both correct roots and identifies the valid solution. Explains that a negative value is not meaningful in this context, though the verification step may be missing or incomplete.
rubric.developing: Solves the equation with significant errors, or obtains only one root. Does not interpret the roots in context, or accepts x = −15 as a valid answer without question.

rubric.criterion: Applying the Quadratic Process to a New Kenyan Context
rubric.excellent: Presents a detailed, accurate, and fully worked second example rooted in a Kenyan context (e.g., a Rift Valley shamba, a Mombasa fishpond, a Nairobi market stall). Correctly forms, solves, and interprets the quadratic equation for the new situation, and comments meaningfully on whether one or both roots are valid.
rubric.proficient: Provides a relevant Kenyan example and forms a correct or near-correct quadratic equation. Solves the problem and gives a contextual interpretation, though the working or explanation may have minor gaps.
rubric.developing: Provides an example that is vague, non-Kenyan, or incorrectly modelled. The quadratic equation formed is inaccurate, or the student cannot solve or interpret it in context.

rubric.excellent: Writes in clear, full sentences throughout. Uses correct mathematical vocabulary consistently (quadratic equation, standard form, roots, factorisation, variable, coefficient, valid/invalid solution). The reflection section shows genuine growth in thinking, identifies a specific misconception that was resolved, and connects quadratic equations to at least one other subject or future topic.
rubric.proficient: Uses mostly correct vocabulary and writes in reasonably clear sentences. The reflection identifies something that was initially confusing and explains the key learning, though connections to other subjects or future topics may be superficial.
rubric.developing: Mathematical vocabulary is limited, missing, or used incorrectly. The reflection is brief, generic ('I learned how to solve quadratic equations'), or does not connect to the phenomenon or to broader applications.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How can writing and solving a quadratic equation help us find unknown dimensions, quantities, and arrangements in real-life situations across Kenya?

lessons.title: Anchoring Phenomenon & Forming Algebraic Expressions
lessons.observed: Teacher presents the anchoring phenomenon: Achieng is arranging chairs in a hall in Kisumu for a harambee event. The number of columns exceeds the number of rows by 7, and the total number of chairs is 120. Students observe that two unknown but related quantities (rows and columns) multiply to give a known product. Teacher should display a physical or drawn grid of chairs and ask students to predict the number of rows before any instruction. Cold-call at least 3 students to share predictions and record these on the Driving Question Board (DQB). Allow 30 seconds of wait time after the prompt: 'What do you notice about the relationship between the rows and columns?'
lessons.learned: Students learn to represent unknown quantities algebraically: if the number of rows is r, then the number of columns is r + 7. This is a foundational skill — teacher should emphasise that choosing the smaller or more basic unknown as the variable (r) simplifies the expression for the related quantity. The product of the two expressions gives the total: r(r + 7) = 120. Pedagogical note: Ensure students understand that r represents a specific, real number of rows — it is not arbitrary. Reinforce that the letter is a placeholder for a value we are trying to find.
lessons.explained: Students explain that when one unknown exceeds another by a fixed amount and their product is known, we can let the smaller quantity equal r and write the larger as r + 7. Multiplying these gives r(r + 7) = 120. Teacher should confirm that this single equation holds all the information needed to solve the problem — both unknowns are expressed in terms of one variable. Connect back to the phenomenon: 'We now have a mathematical sentence that describes Achieng's chair arrangement. Our next step is to learn how to solve it.'

lessons.title: From Expressions to Quadratic Expressions: Recognising and Writing ax² + bx + c
lessons.observed: Teacher guides students to expand the expression r(r + 7) by distributing: r × r = r², and r × 7 = 7r, giving r² + 7r. Students observe that multiplying two linear expressions — one with degree 1 and one with degree 1 — always produces a term with degree 2 (the squared term). Teacher provides 3–4 additional pairs of linear expressions for students to expand (e.g., from Kenyan contexts: length and width of a maize farm plot near Eldoret, sides of a rectangular fish pond at Lake Victoria). Ask students: 'What do all the expanded results have in common?' Allow 20 seconds of wait time, then cold-call 3 students.
lessons.learned: Students learn that the product of two linear expressions always yields a quadratic expression of the standard form ax² + bx + c, where a ≠ 0. The x² (or r²) term arises because x × x = x². Teacher should use colour-coding on the board: highlight the squared term in one colour, the linear term in another, and the constant in a third. Pedagogical note: Students frequently forget to multiply all terms when expanding — teacher should model the 'each term in the first bracket multiplies each term in the second bracket' rule explicitly, using arrows or the FOIL mnemonic as a scaffold.
lessons.explained: Students explain that expanding r(r + 7) gives r² + 7r, and that substituting the known product (120) produces r² + 7r = 120, which rearranges to r² + 7r − 120 = 0. This is now in standard quadratic form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a = 1, b = 7, and c = −120. Teacher should connect explicitly to the anchoring phenomenon: 'Every time we expand Achieng's row-and-column expressions, we get a quadratic equation. This is why the equation type is called quadratic — from the Latin for square, because area (and arrangements) involve squared terms.'

lessons.title: Forming Quadratic Equations from Real-Life Situations
lessons.observed: Teacher presents 2–3 new Kenyan real-life scenarios that generate quadratic equations: e.g., a tea farmer in Kericho whose rectangular plot has a length 5 m more than its width and an area of 84 m²; a matatu operator in Nairobi whose daily passengers exceed daily trips by 4 and whose product is 96. Students observe each scenario, identify the two related unknowns, and attempt to write the equation before instruction. Teacher circulates and notes common errors (e.g., students writing x + 5 = 84 instead of x(x + 5) = 84). Allow 1 minute of independent thinking before pair discussion. Cold-call 4 pairs to share their equations.
lessons.learned: Students learn the three-step process for forming a quadratic equation from a real-life situation: (1) identify the two related unknowns and define a variable for the smaller/simpler one; (2) express the second unknown in terms of the first; (3) write the product (or other relationship) equal to the known total and rearrange to standard form ax² + bx + c = 0. Pedagogical note: Stress that the equation must equal zero in standard form before any solving method is applied. Students often stop at x(x + 5) = 84 — teacher should demonstrate rearranging to x² + 5x − 84 = 0 and explain why this form is necessary for the factorisation methods ahead.
lessons.explained: Students explain that whenever two related unknown quantities are multiplied to give a known total, the resulting equation always contains a squared term and is therefore quadratic. They can now form quadratic equations from diverse Kenyan contexts — farming plots, event seating, market quantities — and write them in standard form. Teacher should ask: 'How does every equation we formed today link back to Achieng's chair problem in Kisumu?' Expected student response: both involve two related unknowns whose product is known, producing the same algebraic structure.

lessons.title: Factorisation of Quadratic Expressions: The Product-and-Sum Method
lessons.observed: Teacher writes x² + 7x − 120 on the board (Achieng's expression) and asks: 'Can we reverse the expansion? Can we write this as a product of two brackets?' Students attempt to guess the brackets before instruction. Teacher then introduces the product-and-sum method with a structured example: find two numbers whose product = −120 (the constant term, c) and whose sum = +7 (the coefficient of x, b). Teacher provides a factor-pair table for students to complete collaboratively for the numbers −120 and +7. Allow 2 minutes of pair work. Cold-call 3 pairs to report candidate factor pairs.
lessons.learned: Students learn the product-and-sum method: for a quadratic x² + bx + c, find integers p and q such that p × q = c and p + q = b, then factorise as (x + p)(x + q). For x² + 7x − 120, the correct pair is p = 15, q = −8 (since 15 × −8 = −120 and 15 + (−8) = 7), giving (x + 15)(x − 8). Pedagogical note: Many students struggle with negative constants. Teacher should dedicate time to the sign rules: if c is negative, the two numbers have opposite signs; if c is positive and b is positive, both numbers are positive; if c is positive and b is negative, both numbers are negative. Use a simple sign-decision chart as a classroom poster.
lessons.explained: Students explain that the product-and-sum method reverses expansion by identifying the two numbers that were originally added (to give bx) and multiplied (to give c) inside the brackets. For Achieng's equation, x² + 7x − 120 = (x + 15)(x − 8). Teacher should verify by re-expanding: (x + 15)(x − 8) = x² − 8x + 15x − 120 = x² + 7x − 120 ✓. Reinforce that factorisation is a tool — its power is revealed in the next lesson when we use it to solve the equation and find the actual number of rows in Achieng's hall.

lessons.title: Solving Quadratic Equations by Factorisation: Finding and Interpreting Both Roots
lessons.observed: Teacher writes the fully factorised equation (x + 15)(x − 8) = 0 on the board and asks: 'If two numbers multiply to give zero, what must be true about at least one of them?' Allow 20 seconds of wait time. Cold-call 3 students. Teacher then demonstrates: if (x + 15)(x − 8) = 0, then either x + 15 = 0, giving x = −15, or x − 8 = 0, giving x = 8. Students observe that a quadratic equation always has two roots. Teacher asks: 'Achieng is arranging real chairs in a real hall. Which root makes sense — x = −15 or x = 8? Why?' Allow 30 seconds of think time before cold-calling.
lessons.learned: Students learn the Zero Product Property: if A × B = 0, then A = 0 or B = 0 (or both). This allows each factor to be set equal to zero independently, yielding two roots. They also learn that real-life context governs which root(s) are valid: a negative number of rows is impossible, so x = −15 is rejected and x = 8 (rows) is accepted. The number of columns is then 8 + 7 = 15. Verification: 8 × 15 = 120 ✓. Pedagogical note: Insist that students always check both roots against the context and write a conclusion sentence. This is a key mathematical practice — sense-making beyond the algebra.
lessons.explained: Students explain that solving by factorisation uses the Zero Product Property to find two roots, and that context determines which root(s) are meaningful. For Achieng's problem, the hall has 8 rows and 15 columns of chairs. Teacher should connect this full solution back to the driving question: 'We started with a real arrangement problem in Kisumu, wrote an algebraic expression, formed a quadratic equation, factorised it, and used the roots to find the actual dimensions. That is the full power of quadratic equations in real life.'

lessons.title: Solving Quadratic Equations by Completing the Square
lessons.observed: Teacher presents a quadratic equation that does not factorise neatly with integers (e.g., x² + 6x − 7 = 0, or a Kenyan context: a rectangular shamba in Nakuru with area 55 m² where the length exceeds the width by 6 m, giving x² + 6x − 55 = 0). Teacher first asks students to attempt factorisation and observes that some equations require an alternative method. Teacher then introduces completing the square: rewrite x² + bx as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)². Demonstrate step by step on the board, inviting students to predict each next step. Cold-call 3 students at each stage. Allow 30 seconds of wait time after posing: 'What do we add to both sides to create a perfect square?'
lessons.learned: Students learn the completing-the-square method: (1) ensure the equation is in the form x² + bx + c = 0 (coefficient of x² is 1); (2) move the constant to the right side; (3) add (b/2)² to both sides to form a perfect square trinomial; (4) write the left side as (x + b/2)²; (5) take the square root of both sides (remembering ±); (6) solve for x. Pedagogical note: Students commonly forget the ± when taking the square root — teacher should highlight this explicitly and explain that it is the source of the two roots. Also ensure students simplify surds or decimals as appropriate, and always check solutions in the original equation.
lessons.explained: Students explain that completing the square is a universal method for solving any quadratic equation of the form x² + bx + c = 0, even when factorisation with integers is not possible. The method transforms the quadratic into a perfect square expression, making it solvable by taking a square root. For Kenyan real-life problems involving area, distance, or quantity, completing the square allows learners to find unknown dimensions precisely. Teacher should connect to the anchoring phenomenon: 'If Achieng's product had not been 120 — say the total chairs were 130 — the equation might not factorise neatly, and completing the square would be our reliable tool.'

lessons.title: Applications and Digital Research: Quadratic Equations in the Real World
lessons.observed: Teacher facilitates a structured research and application session. Students (in groups) explore real Kenyan contexts where quadratic equations arise: seating arrangements for county functions, rectangular agricultural plots in the Rift Valley, profit-maximisation for a mandazi seller in Mombasa, projectile paths in athletics (inspired by Kenyan runners' training drills). Each group is given a scenario card with a quadratic equation to form and solve. Groups also use available digital tools (if accessible) to verify solutions graphically. Teacher circulates, prompts with: 'Where is the quadratic structure in your scenario — what two related unknowns are being multiplied?' Allow 10 minutes of group work before presentations.
lessons.learned: Students learn that the quadratic structure first seen in Achieng's chair problem — (unknown quantity) × (unknown quantity + fixed difference) = known total — recurs across many real-life Kenyan situations: area of rectangular land, total items in a rectangular arrangement, revenue calculations (price × quantity where both relate to the same variable), and even motion problems. Pedagogical note: Emphasise transferability — the algebraic method (form → expand → rearrange → factorise or complete the square → interpret roots in context) is identical regardless of the scenario. Students should see the method as a general problem-solving tool, not a one-off procedure tied only to chairs.
lessons.explained: Students explain how to identify a real-life situation that generates a quadratic equation, form the equation correctly, solve it using an appropriate method (factorisation or completing the square), and interpret the roots in context. Teacher should ask each group: 'How does your scenario connect to our driving question?' Expected response: finding unknown dimensions, quantities, or arrangements in real Kenyan situations is exactly what quadratic equations help us do. Record new insights on the DQB and celebrate examples that extend beyond the original anchoring phenomenon.

lessons.title: Model Building, Consolidation & Final Explanation: The Full Journey of a Quadratic Equation
lessons.observed: Teacher returns to the original anchoring phenomenon — Achieng's 120-chair arrangement in Kisumu — and displays the full DQB, showing how student questions and understanding have evolved across all 8 lessons. Students review their initial predictions from Lesson 1 and compare them with their current knowledge. Teacher asks: 'At the start, how did you try to find the number of rows? How do you solve this now?' Cold-call 4 students. Students then individually attempt a parallel problem (e.g., a school in Eldoret arranges 180 desks in rows where columns exceed rows by 3 — find the number of rows), applying the complete method from start to finish. Allow 8 minutes of independent work.
lessons.learned: Students consolidate the full solution pathway for a quadratic equation arising from a real-life situation: (1) define the variable for the simpler unknown; (2) express the related unknown in terms of the variable; (3) write the product/relationship equal to the known total; (4) expand and rearrange to standard form ax² + bx + c = 0; (5) factorise using the product-and-sum method (or complete the square if needed); (6) apply the Zero Product Property to find both roots; (7) interpret roots in context and reject any that are not valid (e.g., negative dimensions); (8) verify the solution. Pedagogical note: This eight-step pathway should be displayed as a permanent classroom anchor chart. Encourage students to articulate each step verbally — mathematical communication is a core CBE competency.
lessons.explained: Students explain that a quadratic equation of the form x² + 7x − 120 = 0 arises when two related unknown dimensions (such as rows and columns of a chair arrangement) have a known product and a known difference. It is solved by factorising into (x + 15)(x − 8) = 0, applying the Zero Product Property to get x = −15 or x = 8, and then rejecting x = −15 because a negative number of rows has no physical meaning in Achieng's hall. The valid solution, x = 8 rows and 15 columns, satisfies 8 × 15 = 120 ✓. Teacher closes by returning to the driving question: 'How can writing and solving a quadratic equation help us find unknown dimensions, quantities, and arrangements in real-life situations across Kenya?' Students should now be able to answer this question fully, fluently, and with examples drawn from their own Kenyan contexts.
